Existing approaches largely rely on predefined user behaviors, which may miss agent- or domain-specific weaknesses, while failure-oriented search can reduce task success by invalidating the underlying task rather than exposing genuine robustness failures. To fill this gap, we introduce TIPER, a task-integrity-preserving persona evolution method that automatically discovers agent-specific user policies exposing robustness weaknesses while keeping the underlying task valid and solvable. TIPER evolves persistent user personas through reflection-guided behavioral mutations and task-wise Pareto selection under a task-integrity constraint. Across four interactive-agent benchmarks, TIPER yields lower held-out avg@3 scores in all 12 GPT-5.4 settings, with observed reductions of 5.8 to 33.7 percentage points, and in all 28 agent-domain pairs spanning seven agents, with a median observed reduction of 22.9 points. Further analysis yields a behavior-to-failure taxonomy that connects discovered user behaviors to recurring agent failure modes. Together, these results show that TIPER enables more diagnostic robustness evaluation of interactive agents and provides informative failure analysis for future agent robustness improvement. Code repository: https://github.com/UCSB-NLP-Chang/TIPER.

title: AuthGateBench: Benchmarking LLMs as Authorization Gate
abstract: Automated approval systems let coding agents execute high-risk actions with minimal human oversight by delegating the authorization decision to a classifier, typically a large language model (LLM). Such systems, adopted in tools like Claude Code and Codex, remain vulnerable to failure modes such as scope escalation, where the agent takes actions exceeding what the user authorized. Existing benchmarks focus mainly on malicious requests, evaluating refusal under an implicit policy. We introduce AuthGateBench, the first policy-guided benchmark for authorization gating under benign requests. We implement a novel pipeline where an LLM generates contrast pairs with identical action and trajectory but differing request, flipping the label between block and allow. This allows us to assess whether models reason over context rather than the action alone. We further examine whether auxiliary environment signals can help models make better decisions. The resulting benchmark comprises 1,400 instances spanning five failure modes drawn from real-world Claude Code incidents. Evaluations show accuracy degrades unevenly across failure modes as models over-rely on internal safety alignment, and models still block most actions even when explicitly authorized, revealing unstable rather than deterministic decisions; retrospectively retrieved environment signals, however, substantially improve authorization accuracy.

title: ANCHOR: Assessing Naturalistic Constraint Hierarchies and Ordering in Repository-Grounded Agentic Coding
abstract: For repository-grounded coding agents, a functionally correct patch is not necessarily an acceptable one: developers also constrain how the task must be carried out-modification scope, workflow order, validation, tool use, and reporting. This capability, which we call engineering constraint following, remains largely invisible to current evaluations. We introduce ANCHOR (Assessing Naturalistic Constraint Hierarchies and Ordering in Repository-Grounded Agentic Coding), a benchmark built on naturalistic, multilingual repository tasks spanning eight language groups. ANCHOR combines (i) a hierarchical taxonomy of 10 categories and 78 leaf types distilled from real developer interactions, (ii) an automated pipeline that instantiates task-grounded atomic constraints and composes them into typed AND/THEN/PRIORITY relations, and (iii) a trajectory-grounded evaluation framework that checks both the code diff and the execution trajectory with rule-based and LLM judges. Across 19 agent configurations spanning 2 scaffolds and 10 foundation models on 358 tasks, the strongest measured system, Claude Opus 4.8 under Cline, reaches 70.1% atomic compliance and 63.7% relation compliance, while 19.0% of tasks pass every scored checklist item under the strict all-item FCCR criterion. A five-engineer audit of constraints from 50 instances reports 94% feasibility, 94% repository consistency, and 96% realism. In the primary paired set (14 configurations), the mean signed change in task completion after adding constraints is +0.7 percentage points; individual changes vary in both directions. These results distinguish functional success from constraint compliance, with failures concentrated in workflow ordering, tool-use discipline, and reporting, and substantial interactions between models and scaffolds.

title: SpecGuardBench: Can Coding Agents Construct Reliable Validation Harnesses from Natural Language Specifications?
abstract: As coding agents become more capable, tests remain the primary evidence for judging whether their code is correct. Yet passing available tests does not establish that an implementation satisfies its natural language specification. Reliable validation requires checks that faithfully capture the specification and scenarios that thoroughly exercise the code, but current benchmarks provide limited insight into whether agents can construct such evidence themselves. We introduce SpecGuardBench, a benchmark of 291 tasks from 13 real-world repositories, covering 8 types of verification logic such as functional postconditions and interaction protocols. Given a natural language specification, repository context, and a reference implementation, an agent constructs a validation harness comprising executable checks and test scenarios. The checks should reject implementations that violate the specification while accepting those that satisfy it, and the scenarios should thoroughly exercise the code. Across four proprietary and open-weight coding agents, none constructs a harness scored as faithful on the benchmark's implementations for more than 63% of the tasks. The bottleneck lies less in exploring test scenarios than in constructing checks that faithfully reflect the specification. Specifically, the agents show a clear tendency to write checks that mirror the reference implementation rather than the specification, and therefore reject implementations that the specification permits.

title: DuoDiscover: Scaling Autonomous Discovery Beyond the Evaluation Bottleneck
abstract: Evaluation has been central to advances in AI, and it is equally critical to autonomous discovery. Yet scaling autonomous discovery to real-world engineering challenges faces a fundamental bottleneck: the cost of evaluating progress. In real settings, a single true evaluation, such as a full benchmark or serving trace, can take hours, so a search can afford only a handful of true evaluations. We present DuoDiscover, a search system that jointly discovers what to optimize and how to evaluate progress efficiently, through three mechanisms. First, each worker in a fleet of coding agents co-discovers an optimization target and a fast, tailored proxy evaluator, which we call a yardstick. The agent then hill-climbs the yardstick rather than the true evaluation. Second, since search can exploit gaps between a yardstick and the true objective, fidelity tests continually recheck each yardstick's ranking and invalidate any that drift. Third, the fleet is bottom-up, with no central decomposition of the problem. A lightweight orchestrator spawns and terminates agents, briefs running ones, and seeds new agents with others' confirmed work. DuoDiscover enables autonomous optimization from software to chip architecture. We demonstrate DuoDiscover on two repository-level benchmarks and four GPU and TPU kernel suites covering hundreds of kernels. On SWE-fficiency, it doubles the average speedup of human experts. On SOL-Exec, it ranks first on 121 of 235 kernels and in the top three on 212. On the heavily optimized vLLM and SQLite engines, DuoDiscover achieves 1.92$\times$ and 1.38$\times$ gains over the base code. On a CPU microarchitecture optimization task with evaluations of up to 28 hours, DuoDiscover surpasses both AlphaEvolve-based ArchAgent v2 and the best human design, with 1.65$\times$ ArchAgent v2's gain in 16.7 days versus more than 40 days, advancing the frontier of autonomous chip design.

title: CodeLift: Your Test Suite Is Secretly a Dense SWE Curriculum
abstract: The pass-all-test binary reward has become a standard recipe for training software engineering agents, but its sparsity eliminates difference of partially correct patches. The test pass-rate is a natural alternative. However, we find that it is not a reliable indicator of patch quality. A functionality being tested can be covered by either one challenging test or one hundred trivial tests, where the majority might be already satisfied pass-to-pass tests. We introduce CodeLift, a reinforcement learning method that dynamically calibrates pass-rate rewards, turning the test suite into an adaptive curriculum. At each iteration, CodeLift groups tests that kill the same patches and patches that pass the same tests, then gives more weight to test groups that fewer patch groups pass. This reduces the impact of majority simple tests and focuses more on what is still challenging. Within each rollout, CodeLift applies the same scoring rule to repository snapshots, assigning credit to useful actions even when later ones introduce regressions. Experiments on SWE benchmarks show that CodeLift consistently improves pass@1/2/4/8 over binary and pass-rate baselines. Analyses show that CodeLift provides dense, stable learning signals and unlocks the inherent curriculum in the test suite.

title: Do Theorem Provers Need Theorem-Proving Agents? mini-Lean-agent: A Coding-Agent Baseline for Lean
abstract: General-purpose coding agents use standard shell and file interactions, yet formal theorem-proving agents often rely on specialized, ad-hoc tooling. This makes it difficult to determine which components of theorem-proving agents provide benchmark gains: an improved base model, a specialized harness, a specific tool, or a combination of any of them. We introduce mini-Lean-agent, a deliberately minimal agent for Lean tasks whose only model-visible tool is bash. The model must use bash to inspect and edit the repository, search local libraries, invoke Lean, and manage its own intermediate work, while a separate trusted evaluator verifies the final artifact. We compare mini-Lean-agent against AxProverBase and Numina-Lean-Agent on the Putnam 2025 benchmark. Experiments with Gemini 3.8 Flash as the base model show that mini-Lean-agent solves 7/12 problems at \$2 per problem limit, compared with AxProverBase's 4/12. With Astra as the base model, mini-Lean-agent solves 12/12 problems at an average cost of \$1.28 per problem. This suggests that a generic coding agent with a minimal harness can already achieve strong performance on Lean benchmarks. Our results motivate using mini-Lean-agent as a standard baseline when evaluating theorem-proving infrastructure.

title: VulnBump: A Benchmark for Fixing Vulnerable Dependencies in Real Projects While Keeping the Build and Tests Green
abstract: Software composition analysis (SCA) tools report far more vulnerable dependencies than teams fix: in Snyk Open Source production data, 94% of vulnerability findings have a known fixed version, yet only about 10% are resolved. Agentic coding tools could close this gap, but no benchmark evaluates them on vulnerability-driven upgrades in real, runnable projects across ecosystems, verified independently of the agent. We present VulnBump: 307 upgrade tasks covering 2,066 fixable vulnerabilities in 43 repositories across six package managers, matched to Snyk Open Source production vulnerability distributions. An upgrade passes only if, in a fresh container, dependencies resolve, a rescan shows the targeted vulnerabilities fixed, the project builds, and every previously passing test still passes. A non-agentic baseline that only applies Snyk's recommended version passes 46.9% of upgrades; with the same model (Claude Sonnet 5.5), Snyk's Evo Remediation Agent passes 90.2%, Claude Code + Snyk scan 77.5% and Claude Code unaided 59.6%. The agents fail in opposite ways: Claude Code mostly leaves the vulnerability in place, whereas most of Evo Remediation Agent's failures break the build or tests. An SCA scanner is a key tool for agents: Snyk's guidance raises Claude Code's PASS rate by 17.9 percentage points; without it, Claude Code often settles on a still-vulnerable version. Yet knowing the target is not enough: given the same Snyk findings, Evo Remediation Agent's purpose-built harness passes 12.7 points more than Claude Code + Snyk scan. Major framework migrations remain hard for all harnesses. Because the agents keep projects working at similar rates, evaluating remediation quality in dependency upgrades requires verifying the fix, the build and the tests together.

title: StateHarness: Maintaining Evolving Project State for Long-Horizon Coding Agents
abstract: Long-horizon coding requires agents to maintain an evolving view of the project they are changing: what problem is currently being solved, what has already been learned or modified, which other artifacts may be affected, and what work remains unresolved. When this information is scattered across a growing interaction history, local edits can become disconnected from their later consequences and progress can be difficult to carry forward. We introduce StateHarness, a runtime framework that maintains evolving project state without updating model parameters. The working agent records its current problem and hypothesis, important findings and decisions, discovered repository relationships, and unfinished work. Runtime support prompts record updates, searches for callers, tests, and documentation that may be affected by a change, and maintains a compact working brief for subsequent decisions. When behavioral signals accumulate, a separate diagnostic session revisits the recorded history and surfaces overlooked evidence. Across three repository-level evaluations, StateHarness improves task completion and several measures of change consistency. On RefactorBench, full-chain completion increases from 29.4% to 35.3% and cleanup-check accuracy from 87.0% to 95.4%. On five LHTB software-engineering tasks, mean reward improves from 0.427 to 0.576, exceeding LongHorizon-Harness at substantially lower recorded execution cost. On ChainSWE, bug-fix rate increases from 35.1% to 39.5% and residual debt decreases from 60 to 43 items, although pass-to-pass regressions increase. These results show that maintaining project state can improve long-horizon coding while introducing measurable execution and regression trade-offs.

title: ProtoArena: Can AI Agents Discover and Exploit Real-World Cross-Component Protocol Vulnerabilities?
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly used for vulnerability analysis, yet existing benchmarks provide limited coverage of exploitation that depends on interactions among network protocol components. Such vulnerabilities arise from inconsistencies in message interpretation, timing, state, or trust assumptions across participants. We introduce ProtoArena, a black-box, multi-component, dynamic benchmark with 80 cross-component vulnerability-exploitation environments spanning 11 protocol and application domains and 7 attack categories. Tasks are primarily informed by published protocol-attack mechanisms. Agents interact with running systems through scoped interfaces to achieve security-effect objectives without target source code. Three information levels assess guided reproduction, exploitation with mechanism and topology context, and effect-directed black-box exploration. A hybrid verifier combines rule-based checks with LLM review of independently collected traffic and logs. We evaluate five LLMs. Claude Opus 4.8 achieves the highest observed success rates: 48.8% under L1 guidance and 12.5% under effect-directed black-box L3. In a separate DNSBomb optimization experiment, it achieves a peak downstream-response to average query-input byte-rate ratio exceeding 171,000 times. The results show that agents can achieve verifiable exploitation effects in some cross-component environments, but success with limited black-box information remains low and varies across domains and attack categories. All experiments use controlled, explicitly authorized targets; they do not test production systems or disclose previously unknown vulnerabilities.

title: SWEPatchTest: Evaluating Software Tests Beyond Reproduction
abstract: Coding agents use generated tests to decide whether a proposed patch satisfies an issue's requirements. A suite that fails on the buggy program and passes after applying the reference patch can still accept an incorrect patch or reject a correct patch. We introduce SWEPATCHTEST, a test-generation benchmark with 619 tasks from SWE-bench Pro, SWE-bench Multilingual, and DeepSWE and 82,579 candidate patches collected from coding-agent trajectories. By replaying each suite on the buggy and patched codebases, \benchmark jointly measures issue reproduction, acceptance of correct patches, and rejection of incorrect patches. Joint Validation Rate (JVR), which requires all three criteria on the same task, exposes failures hidden by single-reference evaluation: the best-performing configuration achieves only 9.21% JVR despite reproducing the reference transition on 59.29% of tasks. We further use validation scores to select and scale demonstrations for supervised fine-tuning (SFT). The resulting training recipe approximately triples JVR and improves downstream repair across three SWE-bench benchmarks. Patch discrimination thus provides both a diagnostic measure of test quality and an execution-based signal for curating agent training data.

title: Kairos: Transactional Security Enforcement at the System Boundary for LLM Agents
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are becoming an integral part of the software development lifecycle, and the capabilities granted to them allow an agent to act with the user's authority on any resource it can access. The reach that gives an agent its utility is equally available to an attacker who can steer it. Anything an agent ingests can carry an injected instruction, and since the model does not reliably distinguish instructions from data, indirect prompt injection should be mitigated by mediating the effects the agent produces. Such mediation faces a structural difficulty. Legitimate work and the first step of an attack often look alike when an individual action is observed, and what separates them lies later in the trace, so a monitor limited to allow and deny is forced to decide before the evidence accumulates. We present Kairos, a reference monitor at the isolation boundary of an unmodified, opaque agent, where a tool call, a shell command, and a script the agent writes all cross the boundary as the same file and network operations, so that confinement holds regardless of the agent's behavior. A declarative policy that states which sources are trusted decides most effects deterministically and defers the rest, which are held while the agent continues speculatively. A decision oracle with bounded authority, such as a language model or a human, releases or refuses each deferred effect on the trace. Across three benchmarks and three agent models, Kairos outperforms existing defenses in the trade-off between attack success and utility. In particular, on AgentDojo, it reduces attack success from 47.0\% to 2.7\% while its benign utility stays at the level of the undefended agent.

title: CyberArena: Benchmarking AI Agents in Live Symmetric Attack-and-Defense Combat
abstract: AI agents are demonstrating increasingly strong offensive and defensive cybersecurity capabilities in the real world. Current benchmarks mostly evaluate agents in isolation against static targets. Real cyber operations, however, are dynamic and coupled: security postures constantly change as attackers and defenders adapt to each other in real time. Static benchmarks quickly saturate and miss an agent's ability to attack and defend simultaneously under live pressure. To address this gap, we present CyberArena, a dynamic, symmetric adversarial benchmark built around multi-round attack-and-defense combat. In isolated sandboxes, two agents compete under identical rules, acting concurrently as both attackers and defenders over continuously changing services. This converts static targets into evolving, semi-open challenges, directly testing an agent's speed and precision in discovering, exploiting, and patching vulnerabilities. To sustain the benchmark's longevity, an automated agentic pipeline continuously generates, reviews, and validates new environments. Furthermore, because pairwise contests are notoriously hard to quantify, we introduce a dynamical model that maps match dynamics into unified, multidimensional scores across offensive, defensive, and domain-specific capabilities. Evaluating 12 frontier LLM agents across 40 challenges in 466 matches, CyberArena separates model capabilities where single-agent baselines hit a ceiling. The trajectories read like a fight rather than an exam: defenders patch one hole and miss the next and certify repairs on stale evidence, while capable agents think a move ahead, planting backdoors for later rounds and, in one case, writing their own packet sniffer to watch the opponent. Beyond a benchmark, CyberArena serves as an adaptable, scalable experimental platform for future research on cybersecurity agents.

title: OS-Bench: Evaluating SWE Agents on Cross-OS Code Migration
abstract: Language-model (LM) agents are increasingly evaluated on repository-level software engineering (SWE) benchmarks derived from GitHub issues and pull requests. Although these benchmarks cover a broad range of development tasks, they provide limited insight into a common yet technically distinct challenge: migrating an existing implementation from one operating system (OS) to another while preserving behavior on both. We introduce OS-Bench, an executable benchmark for cross-OS code migration between Linux and Windows. Motivated by case studies showing that cross-platform features are frequently implemented on one OS before support is added for another, OS-Bench identifies migration opportunities by comparing execution coverage collected from the same repository on both systems. Platform-specific regions are then verified, organized into five migration scenarios, and transformed into repository-level tasks with target-platform tests and source-platform regression tests. The resulting benchmark contains 140 validated tasks from 111 repositories across C, C++, C#, Go, and Rust, comprising 91 Windows-to-Linux and 49 Linux-to-Windows migrations. We evaluate six models with SWE-agent, Claude Code, OpenHands, and Win-agent. The best configurations achieve only 26.4% success on Linux-target tasks and 20.4% on Windows-target tasks while preserving correctness across both systems. These results indicate that cross-OS migration is a challenging and underexplored capability, and OS-Bench is a testbed for improving platform-aware SWE agents.

title: AgentSafeEvo: Adversarial Co-Evolution for LLM Agent Safety
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents accomplish complex tasks through multi-turn interactions with external tools. However, malicious content embedded in user queries, tool descriptions, or environment observations can manipulate their decisions and induce unsafe actions. Adversarial co-evolution has emerged as an effective approach to strengthening LLM safety, but existing work primarily focuses on language-level safety or indirect prompt injection in web tasks. In this paper, we introduce AgentSafeEvo, a co-evolutionary reinforcement learning framework for agent safety built on an attacker-defender game spanning diverse tasks and attack types. The attacker learns to construct adversarial agent tasks that expose weaknesses in the defender's tool use, while the defender learns to complete tasks safely under these attacks. We further introduce learnability-guided task weighting, which uses within-task defender-reward variability to adjust each task's contribution to attacker and defender updates. Extensive experiments on agent safety and general capability benchmarks demonstrate that our method improves adversarial robustness while maintaining general agent capabilities.

title: BenchChecker: Assessing the Credibility of Bug-Fixing Benchmarks for LLMs
abstract: While Large Language Models (LLMs) show promise for Automatic Program Repair (APR), existing benchmarks suffer from data contamination, in which test samples appear in training sets, artificially inflating performance. To address this, we propose BenchChecker, a framework compatible with both open-source and closed-source models that supports more credible evaluation by detecting such contamination. Grounded in the observation that persistent patches likely remain in recent repository snapshots used for training, BenchChecker employs a forensics-based two-stage detection process using only textual model outputs together with public repository history. The first stage conducts a repository presence test by probing the model with code prefixes to infer training inclusion; the second stage performs a patch presence test to verify patch persistence via similarity alignment and test-suite verification. Evaluations using StarCoder-15B, StarCoder2-15B, and CodeGen2-16B trained on The Stack v2 demonstrate that BenchChecker achieves robust detection with AUC scores around 0.9 across six benchmarks. Furthermore, applying BenchChecker to SWE-bench Verified and Multi-SWE-bench reveals that filtering contaminated samples reduces the reported resolution rates of most LLMs by more than 20% relative to the original rates on medium-difficulty tasks.

title: Mission (Im)Possible: Towards Autonomous Discovery of Autopilot Logic Flaws in Open-Source Drone Frameworks
abstract: Autonomous drones are increasingly deployed in safety-critical tasks, yet their autopilot software can still contain subtle logic flaws that lead to unsafe behaviors. These flaws are difficult to discover with existing techniques because they often depend on semantic relationships across modules, commands, and runtime state, and rarely manifest as crashes or detectable failures. With recent advances in LLMs, we observe that, when equipped with essential domain knowledge and carefully crafted context, LLMs demonstrate strong capabilities in understanding the high-level semantics of autopilot systems, making them suitable for logic flaw discovery. However, LLMs are limited by their context and can be biased to the vulnerabilities frequently occurs in training dataset, while logic flaws often require higher-level semantic bug oracles to identify their existence. To bridge the gap, we present Impossible Mission Finder (IMF), a multi-agent system combining static analysis, dynamic execution and log analysis, that supports fully automated identify, test, and validate logic flaws in autonomous vehicles. IMF primarily contains three LLM agents, it first uses the auditor agent to propose logic flaw hypothesis based on carefully-crafted program slicing, then it launches tester agents to write and execute test cases for each candidate, and finally it spawns the log analyzer agent to validate the execution log against the flaw hypothesis. This enables IMF dynamically validate bug oracles in a case-by-case manner, making it suitable for discovering logic flaws that do not have a unified pattern. We evaluated IMF on two widely used open-source autopilot systems, PX4 and Ardupilot, leading to 105 previously unknown logic flaws, that can cause unsafe behaviors including mission interruption failures, invalid actions, entering into restricted fly zones etc.

title: Temporal Adaptive Fine-Tuning for Code Comprehension
abstract: Repository-level code comprehension question answering (QA) supports developer reasoning over functionality and usage distributed across codebases. However, repository-specialized large language models (LLMs) can become misaligned as code evolves. We study this challenge as temporal repository adaptation: acquiring new knowledge, suppressing obsolete, retaining still-valid, and preserving semantically neighboring knowledge. Existing retrieval, fine-tuning, and model-editing methods address only parts of this problem. We propose Temporal Adaptive Fine-Tuning (TAFT), a novel adaptation approach that treats repository transitions as supervision. TAFT derives temporally grounded QA data from repository transitions, pairs newly valid with obsolete knowledge through preference optimization, and replays transition-conditioned retention examples to preserve still-valid knowledge. We evaluate TAFT on an augmented temporal SWE-bench dataset comprising 255,295 QA entries across ten temporal slices, comparing deferred (Baseline), per-slice retrained (Baseline-Batched), and variants with knowledge anchors along four dimensions: updated knowledge, obsolete-answer suppression, retention, and neighbor stability. TAFT consistently outperforms both the deferred and batched baselines, with an average relative improvement of 18% in updated/suppressed knowledge accuracy, doubled retention accuracy, and roughly 1.5 times the neighbor accuracy. With directly supplied knowledge anchors, TAFT-KANT further improves mean updated/suppressed, retention, and neighbor accuracy over TAFT by 3.55%, 8.35%, and 13.00%, respectively. Overall, TAFT demonstrates its effectiveness across all evaluated areas, effectively enabling code comprehension QA alignment with repository evolution.

title: The Code of Theseus: Can Agents Rebuild Software from Recovered Design Documents?
abstract: LLM agents increasingly design a system before implementing it, yet the data to train and evaluate them centres on implementation and testing: requirements and design artefacts are often missing, outdated or private. Source code, in contrast, is abundant. Prior work recovers architecture documentation by feeding LLMs the source code or letting agents explore it, which saturates the context, does not scale to many repositories, and yields a single artefact rather than aligned ones. We present a framework that recovers aligned stakeholder intent, requirements and architecture from a compact repository representation, a static dependency graph and key contextual files, and release the artefacts of 10,764 Java, Python, C/C++ and C# repositories as a dataset. An LLM judge rates the artefacts of three generators as clear and internally consistent, but less reliably correct and at the right level of abstraction. To test whether the artefacts carry the design, we pose a software Ship of Theseus: a coding agent rebuilds 29 Commit0 libraries from the intent alone or with the recovered requirements and architecture, given only an interface contract and part of the tests. The artefacts do not significantly change the held-out pass rate (33.7% vs. 35.8%), but bring the rebuilt module structure significantly closer to the original (module F1 from 0.54 to 0.63), with either generator and even with concise artefacts. Recovered artefacts thus convey design that tests do not capture, offering a scalable source of design-level data for agents that design before they implement, and the round trip measures this without human references.

title: SWE-Stream: Scaling Executable Training Data for SWE Agents via Progressive Construction and Elastic Streaming
abstract: Software engineering agents have advanced rapidly, but scaling their training remains constrained by the limited availability of high-quality executable tasks. Development histories contain valuable signals for constructing such tasks, yet they often require substantial reconstruction due to incomplete environments, missing tests, and inconsistent artifacts. We present SWE-Stream, a system for scaling executable SWE training data through progressive construction and elastic streaming execution. SWE-Stream progressively validates and refines task candidates, reusing existing artifacts when possible and applying targeted completion only when necessary. An elastic scheduler asynchronously coordinates construction stages under shared resource constraints, adapting execution budgets based on observed workload demands. Using development histories from 10,728 repositories across six programming languages, SWE-Stream constructs 80,874 validated tasks and collects 118,688 successful trajectories. Fine-tuning Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking-2507 on these trajectories achieves resolve rates of 69.0%, 49.3%, and 45.42% on SWE-bench Verified, Multilingual, and Pro, respectively. In a controlled comparison with approximately matched training budgets, SWE-Stream achieves a 45.6% resolve rate on SWE-bench Verified, outperforming three existing data sources. Moreover, its streaming construction strategy improves efficiency, delivering $1.45\times$ the accepted-task throughput of batch construction and accepting 13.2% more tasks than fixed-limit streaming.

title: From Training to Escalation: Forensic Analysis and Local Recreation of RL/RLHF-Induced Privilege Escalation in AI Agents (CVE-2026-65616)
abstract: Mid-2026 reporting on autonomous AI evaluation incidents claimed that frontier large language model (LLM) agents escaped server containment through emergent coordination and cloud infrastructure attacks. This paper contextualizes those claims through forensic analysis and containerized recreation of both the Highly Persistent Internal Model (HPIM) training-case conditions and the Phase One privilege escalation targeting internal package repositories during OpenAI's ExploitGym evaluations. We recreate the configuration of the OpenAI-provided training example and reproduce the cryptographic verification bypass (CVE-2026-65616) in isolated repository servers, where misconfigured systems enabled token forgery and privilege escalation through basic HTTP requests, Python, and JavaScript. Crucially, the training-example conditions and the Phase One (and later) misconfigurations share the same exploitable patterns. Our analysis explains how Zero Trust Architecture principles neutralize this shared attack vector. Contemporary AI risks derive directly from training and deployment conditions in ambivalent learning environments lacking adequate containment measures.

title: CausalEvo: Causal Skill Self-Evolution for Health LLM Agents
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents for health can accumulate reusable textual skills from task feedback, such as calculation criteria, measurement time points, and formula units. Deciding which skills to retain is consequential: useful rules improve later answers, while faulty generalizations propagate errors. We propose CausalEvo, a method for causal skill self-evolution that estimates the relative effects of deliberately changed skill sets while holding the model weights, feedback cases, and rule count fixed. At each evolution step, a frozen LLM proposes candidate rules, which are pooled with the incumbent skills so that the current skill set remains a feasible choice. Paired skill replacements against shared background rules are scored on the same feedback cases; least squares converts the score differences into relative skill values, and the top-ranked rules are retained, favoring incumbents on ties. A decision-loss bound separates candidate support, approximation, and estimation errors. On six MedCalc-Bench-Verified tasks with 120 held-out cases, CausalEvo achieves 60.00% accuracy, compared with 55.83% for SkillOpt and 51.67% without skills. Across the recorded training configurations, which use different optimization budgets, it consumes 55.6% fewer training tokens than SkillOpt. Gains concentrate in particular calculations alongside regressions on others, and paired accuracy intervals include zero. CausalEvo turns task feedback into controlled decisions about skill retention and replacement. Project repository: https://github.com/txbrook/CausalEvo

title: Skip the Compressor: Coding Agents Fix More Issues When They Pick Whole Files
abstract: A coding agent works on repositories that can be far larger than its context window can hold. Prompt compressors and retrievers offer solutions to this problem, but patching an issue needs two things at once: the files that must change, and their code exactly as written, since the model must reproduce the lines it edits. Retrievers rank code by its similarity to the issue rather than by whether it must change, and compressors delete text to fit the budget. We show that at an equal token budget, an agent resolves more issues when the budget goes to choosing which files to show verbatim, as our simple selector CQ2-CARE does, than when it goes to pruning tokens or retrieving chunks. We fit every context to the same per-issue budget on 300 recent SWE-rebench issues and grade each patch with the benchmark's tests. With GPT-5.6 and Claude Opus 5, CQ2-CARE resolves 43.7% and 46.7% of the issues, 6.3 points more than the best of three compressors with either model, and 9.3 and 12.7 points more than the best of three retrievers. CQ2-CARE even resolves more issues than two methods trained for issue resolution, SweRank (by 0.7 and 1.7 points) and SWE-Pruner (by 2.0 and 7.3). Our analysis shows the defects of the baseline methods: retrievers often miss the files to edit, and compressors keep them but alter their text, so fewer patches apply. Exact-file selection needs no compression model and shows every line as the repository has it, so the model can quote the code it edits.

title: PRIME: Towards Verifiable Evidence-Grounded Reasoning in LLM Agents
abstract: LLM agents are used to check records against an organization's requirements, for example whether a vulnerability report is ready for investigation. Requirements often allow several ways to be met, such as a severity rating with a curator-reviewed advisory or a published advisory link. Agents fail by accepting a report after a required check has failed, or by settling for a weaker conclusion without trying another way that could still succeed. We introduce PRIME (Precommitted Rules for Inference from Minimal Evidence). Before checking, it fixes evidence routes specifying how each conclusion may be justified. A separate program records each check result and refuses any conclusion the results do not justify. It also points the agent to checks that could justify a stronger conclusion, or runs them itself. PRIME reports only conclusions authorized by its rules and ledger. With correct requirements, exact checks at known locations, and sufficient budget at stopping, completion reaches the strongest supported conclusion. On 480 public-record tasks, an agent shown the requirements reported unjustified conclusions on 26.7% of tasks, while PRIME reported none. Its directions and added checks raised the average score for justified conclusions from 30.1, with refusal alone, to the maximum of 59.2 out of 100.

title: Agentic Interpretation: Harness-Governed Evidence Construction for Software Agents
abstract: Software agents answer behavioral questions about code, such as whether a patch passes tests or which lines caused a failure. These tasks require repository-wide evidence, yet most scaffolds leave intermediate findings in free-form trajectories, making them hard to reuse and easy to disconnect from final answers. We present Agentic Interpretation (AgInt), a framework for harness-governed evidence construction. The model proposes typed records, while a deterministic harness admits, grades, and persists them, reports unresolved requirements, and licenses answers under task-specific rules. The resulting certificate gives the model persistent external state and leaves an auditable decision record. Formally, append-only certificate states form a grounding lattice ordered by record inclusion, where each admitted record extends the state by union. We evaluate AgInt with four models on SWE-bench-Live and DeepSWE for patch acceptance and Defects4J and GitBug-Java for fault localization. AgInt outperforms the plain agent and Agentic Code Reasoning on all reported patch-acceptance metrics and ranks responsible lines higher while inspecting fewer irrelevant lines in fault localization. For GLM-5, reject-class F1 rises from 0.256 to 0.543 on SWE-bench-Live, All@1 rises from 0.140 to 0.400 on Defects4J, and wasted inspected lines fall from 31.5 to 11.7 on GitBug-Java. A matched-template control separates the mechanism: the persistent scaffold drives most fault-localization gains, while the certificate body and gate govern patch-acceptance calibration. With execution licensed, AgInt produces harness-reproduced witnesses for 293 of 475 null-dereference candidates versus 253 for a matched shell agent, and 62 of 117 resource-leak candidates versus 58. Across reported efficiency measurements, it uses 35% fewer executions and reduces cost per candidate by 59%.

title: Agentic Dependency Transformations: Lessons from an Exploratory Case Study of Flask
abstract: Modern software relies heavily on third-party libraries, requiring maintainers to balance the benefits of reuse against dependency-related maintenance and risk. We define dependency transformation as an emerging approach in which an AI coding agent alters how a repository handles external dependencies. Local reimplementation is one transformation strategy that recreates required functionality as local code; dependency transformation is broader and may include other strategies. In this emerging-results paper, we report an exploratory case study of Flask to explore dependency transformation strategies. We design experiments that show how available context shapes an agent's dependency discovery and iterative transformation of dependencies. The case yields five preliminary lessons. These lessons and the five-part research agenda position dependency transformation as an emerging research direction and motivate explicit transformation contracts, provenance constraints, preservation requirements, and independent validation criteria.

title: The Role of Agentic Instruction Categories for Code Generation: A Study of Five Python Libraries
abstract: Agentic coding systems increasingly rely on repository-level agent files, such as AGENTS.md, to communicate project knowledge and developer intent. However, it remains unclear which categories of agent instructions enable efficient agent-file generation and accurate code generation. We evaluate five instruction categories: Repository Overview, Function Description, Implementation Detail, Testing, and Reconstruction Steps, across all 31 non-empty combinations using two Large Language Models (LLMs), Gemma 4 and GPT-5.4, and five human-written Python libraries. Our study addresses two research questions, comprising five sub-questions, on agent file generation and code generation. Results show that the number of instructions alone does not determine token usage for agent-file generation, with substantial variation across models and libraries. Although most AI-generated libraries compiled successfully regardless of the instruction combination, functional correctness remained limited. No Gemma 4 variant passed all tests, whereas 12.99% of GPT-5.4 variants did. Function Description achieved Gemma 4's highest partial-pass rate, while Reconstruction Steps achieved GPT-5.4's highest full-pass rate. For structural similarity to human-written code, Reconstruction Steps was most frequently associated with libraries closest to the originals in Lines of File and total Cyclomatic Complexity, while Testing and Reconstruction Steps were jointly most frequent for File Count and Function Count.

title: OPRD: On-Policy Reminder Distillation for Long-Horizon Coding Agents
abstract: Reliable repository-level coding requires agents not only to generate correct code but also to preserve constraints and respond to tool feedback across long interactions. However, our diagnostic analysis shows that agents often fail to act on relevant information already available in context, while final Pass/Fail outcomes provide only sparse process supervision. We introduce On-Policy Reminder Distillation (OPRD), which combines Multi-Scope Reminder supervision with outcome-based routing on reminder-free student rollouts. Successful rollouts provide autoregressive self-imitation targets, whereas failed rollouts receive Reminder-conditioned reverse-KL supervision from a teacher that re-evaluates the same student-generated prefixes. A Global Reminder converts final-test diagnostics into trajectory-level guidance, while Turn-local Reminders apply only to the next decision following the relevant environment observation. The teacher and student share a two-stage initialization from Coding SFT and Instruction-Following (IF) SFT. At inference, the student operates without Reminders. On SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench Pro, and SWE-bench Multilingual, OPRD improves the benchmark-averaged task resolution rate by 11.3 points over the open-source Qwen3.5-4B base model. Under the same diagnostic protocol, it reduces the aggregate error-event count from 446 to 222, a 50.2% reduction.

title: AgentPerturb: Evaluating LLM Agent Robustness under Controlled Interaction Perturbations
abstract: Real-world tasks are often complex and noisy, posing substantial challenges for LLM agents. Yet existing evaluations lack a systematic framework for jointly characterizing potential perturbation targets and types. We use this two-dimensional view to conduct a unified study that quantifies the robustness of current frontier models, traces the mechanisms behind perturbation-induced failures, and draws implications for robustness-oriented training. Through controlled evaluations on APEX-Agents and Toolathlon, we find that perturbations consistently degrade performance, while the dominant vulnerabilities vary across task environments. Trajectory-level analysis reveals that agents rarely recognize altered inputs and often propagate corrupted information without verification. A focused cost analysis further shows that successful perturbed trajectories can require substantially more computation. These findings motivate training objectives that cover diverse forms of noise and reward verification, uncertainty awareness, and recovery. We provide a rigorous benchmark-construction pipeline. Code and data will be released at https://github.com/xuyj233/AgentPerturb.

title: CodeHealth Predicts the Token Cost of Agentic Code Review: A Pre-Registered Study of 465 Agent-Authored Pull Requests
abstract: Context: Organizations increasingly delegate code review to multi-agent large language model (LLM) pipelines billed per token. Low code quality raises human maintenance effort, but its effect on agent review cost has not been measured. Objective: We test whether baseline CodeHealth predicts the token cost of agentic review and fix beyond pull request (PR) footprint. Method: In a pre-registered observational study, we sampled 465 agent-authored PRs from 246 repositories in AIDev, jointly stratified by CodeHealth and footprint under repository caps. A frozen five-agent review-and-fix pipeline processed every PR with three different LLMs. Per LLM, we fitted a mixed model of log tokens on CodeHealth and log PR footprint, with a repository random intercept. Results: For all three LLMs the CodeHealth coefficient was negative, with 95% CI excluding zero; each CodeHealth point was associated with 3.5% to 6.1% lower token cost. CodeHealth was unrelated to PR footprint, so PR size does not explain the association. Two of three registered smells predicted fix cost; batch fixing left median CodeHealth unchanged. Exploratory analyses located the association in the review stage, where agents iterated more on unhealthy code without writing more comments. Adjusting for the size of the scored files absorbed the association, which we interpret as mediation by file size. Conclusions: A quality metric calibrated against human maintainability also predicts the inference cost of multi-agent review and fix. The effect is modest per point and not carried by PR size, so the refactoring case extends to agent-reviewed code when it changes structure and file size, not only the score. Data Availability: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22127920

title: Benchmarking and Enhancing Design-Aware Code Review in the Linux Kernel
abstract: Code review often requires reasoning beyond local correctness. In mature software systems, reviewers must recognize design trade-offs introduced by a proposed change, compare alternative solutions, and reason about their compatibility with project-specific constraints. We refer to this problem as design-aware code review. However, existing automated review approaches primarily focus on defects and correctness, while the design knowledge accumulated in historical review discussions remains difficult to reuse. To address these challenges, we present DesignLore, a knowledge-augmented approach that extracts design decisions from historical review discussions, organizes them into an adaptive design taxonomy, and reuses relevant historical knowledge to guide code review. We further construct DesignReviewBench, a benchmark derived from real patch-review histories for systematically evaluating design-aware code review. Our evaluation shows that design-aware review remains challenging for current coding agents, with the strongest baseline achieving an F1 of only 0.213 on design trade-off detection. In comparison, DesignLore achieves an F1 of 0.259, a 21.6% relative improvement, and consistently delivers gains across different agent systems and backbone. These results highlight the importance of design-aware review and demonstrate the potential of recovering and reusing historical design knowledge to support it.

title: Priming Base Models for Agentic Post-Training: An Open Midtraining Recipe
abstract: Frontier models, general-purpose and domain-specific alike, now include a midtraining stage between pretraining and post-training, but little has been published about how this stage is built. We present an open midtraining recipe that primes base models for agentic post-training, and we show its effectiveness on two Nemotron models of different sizes. Pretraining typically runs at short context and sees almost no agent interactions, while SFT data is mostly synthetic, and very long SFT stages can hurt the model's later RL trainability. Our midtraining stage sits between the two. It trains at 256K context for hundreds of billions of tokens on a diverse mixture of natural software-engineering data like packed repositories, pull requests, commit histories, and build logs together with a small share of agentic traces. On Nemotron 3.5 Lightning, 500B midtraining tokens improve SWE-bench Verified from 60.7 to 64.5, SWE-bench Multilingual from 55.8 to 62.8, and SWE-bench Pro from 32.0 to 35.5 after identical full SFT. On the larger Nemotron 3.5 Super, 280B midtraining tokens improve DeepSWE, a harder benchmark of long-horizon tasks, from 11.7 to 15.7 and SWE-bench Verified from 72.9 to 74.3 after identical full SFT. Midtraining also improves robustness across agent harnesses on both models. We report the ablations behind the recipe and an evaluation protocol built on short fixed SFT runs, since base-model proxy metrics did not correlate reliably with post-training results.

title: WEAVE: Weaving Real-World Code Evolution into Dependency-Structured Tasks for Benchmarking and Training Code Agents
abstract: Real-world software engineering rarely consists of isolated changes. Features, migrations, and systematic fixes often unfold across multiple pull requests (PRs), requiring coordinated modifications across a repository. Yet most executable repository-level benchmarks retain a single issue or PR as the task unit, while existing multi-PR settings rely on coarse aggregation and structure-agnostic evaluation. This mismatch obscures dependencies among changes and limits progress measurement and learning signals for long-horizon code agents. We introduce WEAVE, a framework that transforms verified PR histories into executable, dependency-structured tasks. WEAVE leverages repository-calibrated typed change loci to organize related PRs into bounded DAGs and instantiate each as a unified executable task. We further introduce Graph Credit, a deterministic, test-grounded metric that measures dependency-consistent partial progress and supports dense, verifiable rewards for reinforcement learning. Experiments on task construction, agent evaluation, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning show that WEAVE yields coherent executable tasks, enables more faithful progress measurement than flat scoring, and provides effective supervision and verifiable rewards for training code agents.

title: The Model Knows Better: Defending Medical Multi-Agent Systems Against Prompt Injection
abstract: Medical multi-agent systems, in which LLM agents discuss a case, are increasingly studied for clinical decision support. Prompt injection, text that an attacker adds to a model's input, can manipulate LLMs into wrong decisions. How it affects these systems, and how to protect them, remains unclear. Across two systems, two model families and three benchmarks, a single injected passage succeeds in up to 61% of cases, and collaboration does not consistently protect against it. Existing defenses help only partly: they miss injections that look like ordinary clinical text. Yet when asked to check the injected text against the patient's findings, a model that followed the injection usually rejects it. We therefore propose a training-free defense that verifies the clinical judgments behind the system's decision. Following clinical practice, it separates the patient's findings from clinical judgments, such as diagnoses, recommendations and instructions, and checks each judgment against the findings alone, so the decision rests only on supported judgments. Our defense outperforms all baselines on every benchmark, lowering attack success on MedQA to 4-7% while maintaining accuracy on cases without an attack, and remains effective with a medical model and against defense-aware and adaptive attacks.

title: TokenEconomizer: Experience-Driven Black-Box Cost Control for Coding Agents
abstract: Advances in frontier coding agents have sharply increased the token costs of AI-assisted software engineering. Their token efficiency is typically evaluated on isolated tasks, whereas real-world developers use them to continuously build, update, and maintain large-scale projects. This mismatch motivates us to evaluate agents over sequences of realistic coding tasks, where we find that agents exhibit recurring environment-dependent token costs that existing methods struggle to reduce. To minimize these costs, we introduce TokenEconomizer, an external controller that cuts environment-specific token costs over a sequence of tasks. These cuts come from determining (i) which operational micro-skills to inject, (ii) which persistently irrelevant tools to prune, and (iii) when to intervene in unproductive failure loops. Across Claude Code, Codex, and GitHub Copilot CLI paired with frontier models, TokenEconomizer reduces the average token cost by 18.4-30.9% with comparable task success. Savings hold in every repository under every tested agent-model setting and generalize to diverse domains such as sequential web development and security auditing, where costs fall by 6.4-21.2% depending on task structure. Our work establishes adaptive black-box cost control as a promising direction for reducing token costs of coding agents in realistic settings.

title: Between Spoilers and Guesswork: Avoiding Over-Specification in Coding Benchmarks
abstract: Benchmarks drive AI progress, but are hampered by task under-specification and over-specification. Task under-specification causes guesswork, where solutions have to make things up, or worse, resort to contamination or reward hacking. Task over-specification causes spoilers, where solutions can bypass some of the harder steps the benchmark was supposed to measure. Since future-looking benchmarks should be difficult, over-specification reduces a benchmark's shelflife of community adoption. Repository-level coding benchmarks have helped the field progress but experience unnecessary churn due to both over- and under-specification. For instance, SWE-bench Pro, FEA-bench, Doc2Feat-bench, and Multi-SWE-bench all tackle under-specification by augmenting task statements with hints derived from ground truth. We show that leaking ground-truth information into the task statement causes over-specification in some of these benchmarks. We experiment with various specification levels, trying to thread the needle between spoilers and guesswork. Based on these results, we recommend techniques for deriving parsimonious hints. We will release our hints so the community can obtain more reliable signals from popular benchmarks.

title: From Approval to Abuse: Privilege Escalation Attacks on Harness-Protected Coding Agents
abstract: Coding agents use execution harnesses to constrain the consequences of prompt injection by enforcing permission boundaries. These systems deterministically intercept any out-of-sandbox action and prompt the user for approval. To reduce approval fatigue, users can approve allow-rules proposed by the agent, after which any future action matching the rule is allowed without a prompt. In this work, we show that this mechanism introduces a new risk: untrusted context can influence the permissions presented for approval, with consequences extending beyond the immediate task. We investigate privilege escalation targeting this permission-update process. Specifically, adversarial context planted in a repository can reliably steer an agent performing a routine task into requesting a plausibly justified, yet dangerously broad allow-rule. If the user approves the request, the saved rule can effectively blind the harness, enabling adversaries to execute malicious actions that would otherwise require approval, without triggering human oversight. Across production platforms, including Claude Code and Codex CLI, we demonstrate that agents successfully elicit the target allow-rules in 58% of experimental instances. Once acquired, these rules exhibit a massive semantic blast radius, covering 56.9% of category-specific capability test cases. To further quantify the downstream risk, we show that conditional on rule approval, our exploit achieves verified, silent goal completion in 47 of the 58 eligible instances (81.0%), undermining the safety promise of human-in-the-loop oversight.

title: Trojan Horse: Automated Repository Poisoning against Coding Agents
abstract: Coding agents are increasingly capable with autonomy, which exposes them to repository-level poisoning. Existing red-teaming studies remain restricted to manual selection for malicious payload locations and fixed disguise strategies, which cannot represent realistic repository poisoning. We present TrojanForge, the first automated framework for repository poisoning. TrojanForge parses repository structure through abstract syntax trees (AST) and maps agent execution traces onto AST nodes. A security review agent ranks these candidates and selects the least conspicuous ones for payload mounting. Then, through adversarial play with the target agent, TrojanForge iteratively refines disguise strategies by inverting the causes of agent detection, and transfers accumulated success experience across repositories. We further construct TrojanBench, a benchmark of 384 poisoned repositories spanning 6 domains and 9 programming languages. Extensive experiments show that TrojanForge achieves a stable poisoning success rate of over 60% with backdoor injection exceeding 90%. Comprehensive evaluation on TrojanBench across 4 harnesses and 12 models reveals that even commercial agents fail to defend against repository-level poisoning.

title: MobileInject: Evaluating Reasoning-to-Action Security of MLLM-Based Mobile Agents under Cross-Modal Consistency Injection
abstract: Multimodal large language model (MLLM)-based mobile agents are rapidly evolving from conversational assistants into autonomous systems that perceive, reason over, and act on smartphone environments. This capability also exposes a new security risk: adversaries can embed malicious objectives in cross-application mobile content and steer agent behavior through indirect multimodal injection. Although prompt injection has been studied in desktop and web settings, its cross-modal properties in mobile ecosystems remain poorly understood, and existing security analyses are still limited. To close this gap, we introduce MobileInject, the first benchmark for evaluating mobile agents against multimodal injection attacks and reasoning-to-action security risks. MobileInject provides a high-fidelity interactive mobile evaluation framework covering 11 scenarios, 9 security-risk categories, and 108 executable risk instances. It further introduces Cross-Modal Consistency Injection to exploit corroboration across modalities, two enhanced attack methods, Multi-Role Collaborative Deception and Reasoning-Camouflage Injection, to intensify trust manipulation and reasoning hijacking, and a Reasoning Security Diagnosis Framework for fine-grained failure analysis. Systematic experiments show that mobile agents are broadly vulnerable to multimodal injection, and that many failures stem from reasoning hijacking at early stages. These findings establish MobileInject as a systematic cross-modal benchmark for studying and improving the security of mobile agents. Code release details are provided in the Appendix Open Science section.

title: S-GAP: Stealthy Graph Attack Primitives for Graph Large Language Models
abstract: Graph Large Language Models (GraphLLMs) enable powerful semantic understanding and reasoning over Text-Attributed Graphs (TAGs), while their semantic reasoning may exhibit vulnerabilities to perturbations in node text and graph structure under adversarial attack evaluation. Existing attacks typically construct textual and structural perturbations in separate stages guided by distinct realization intents. However, this separation results in attack-intent fragmentation, causing semantic incoherence between the two perturbation types, thereby undermining attack stealth and making them easier for GraphLLMs to identify and disregard, ultimately weakening attack effectiveness. To avoid attack-intent fragmentation, we propose the Graph Attack Primitive (GAP), an atomic semantic representation that unifies textual and structural perturbations under a coherent attack intent. By carefully calibrating the semantic composition of a GAP, we can achieve strong attack effectiveness while maintaining sufficient attack stealth. Furthermore, we introduce S-GAP (Stealthy GAP), a multi-agent framework that iteratively refines the semantic content of the GAP. The framework unifies GAP planning and realization and continuously refines this process through surrogate evaluation and textual feedback. Extensive experiments across four datasets, three GraphLLMs, and two attack settings show that S-GAP improves ASR over the strongest baselines by 7.02% on average while producing more relationally plausible perturbations, exposing critical vulnerabilities in current GraphLLMs and motivating more robust defenses.

title: The Window Is in the Reasoning: When LLM Agents Decide to Follow Prompt Injections
abstract: LLM agents that read untrusted content can be hijacked by prompt injections. Runtime monitors that try to catch a hijack before the agent acts, and benchmarks that score each task with a single run, share an assumption: whether an agent follows an injection is settled when the injection is read. We test this assumption with branching rollouts that replay an episode exactly up to the step at which the agent reads an injection and then resample the rest of the episode many times, splitting the outcome variance into a part fixed at read time and a part decided afterwards. Across four AgentDojo suites, a Qwen3 agent without thinking is largely decided at read time (0.91 of the outcome variance lies between states); with thinking on, this share drops to 0.62 (95% CI of the drop [-0.38, -0.22]), in the same direction for three attack templates and two success labels. How much is fixed at read time is a property of the model that the same measurement reveals, and thinking lowers the attack success rate of Qwen3 but raises it for two other models. Resampling from reasoning prefixes shows that the decision forms gradually as the agent reasons. Zero-shot chain-of-thought monitors built on cheaper models miss much of what is already decided, whereas stronger monitors, and a lookahead monitor that judges simulated next actions, come close to what the prefix determines. Finally, single-run labels of thinking agents disagree with a rerun up to 35% of the time, so benchmarks need repeated runs per task.

title: Enforcing Code Reasoning in Agentic Scaffold for More Effective Issue Resolution
abstract: Reasoning is central to ReAct-based programming agents, yet whether and how they reason about code remains unclear. We study 7,955 issue-resolution trajectories from six single- and multi-agent scaffolds across four programming languages on SWE-bench-Verified, SWE-bench-Pro, and SWE-bench-Lite. We identify 12 forms of code reasoning in 66.95% of trajectories. Code reasoning is associated with higher resolution rates, and its intensity increases with task complexity. However, it remains largely unguided: agents may focus on surface-level symptoms during localization, fail to refine near-correct patches, overlook issue requirements, and generate tests with limited behavioral diversity. To address these limitations, we propose DeskCheck, an agentic scaffold that systematically guides code reasoning throughout repository-level issue resolution. DeskCheck simulates execution paths to localize root causes, simulates candidate patches to refine near-misses, audits patches against issue requirements, and reasons about corner-case inputs and expected outputs before generating tests. On 731 SWE-bench-Pro instances, DeskCheck improves resolution rates over mini-SWE-Agent and Claude Code by 6.29% to 10.53%, at an additional cost of $0.02-$0.28 per instance (average: $0.14). Per-phase analyses show higher method-level localization recall, more successful repairs of imprecisely localized issues, and better detection of missed corner cases in near-correct patches. Exact McNemar tests show statistically significant improvements across all subject LLMs (p < 10^-10), while repeated experiments support robustness to agent nondeterminism. These findings motivate systematic code reasoning as a means of improving programming agents.

title: Who Verifies the Builder? Toward Independent Assurance for Agent-Produced Software
abstract: Coding agents can now implement a specification, write and run tests, repair failures, and declare the result ready for release. When the same agentic system produces both the software and the evidence of its correctness, a passing test suite is no longer independent evidence: visible tests become an optimization target, code and tests may share one misinterpretation of the specification, and the builder's own tests may simply be incomplete. This paper argues that agent-produced software requires an assurance plane that is structurally independent of the build plane. We characterize four gaps between stakeholder intent and production (requirement, conformance, evaluation, and model gaps) and identify which of them verification can close. We propose a framework that separates building from verifying, introduces a Verification Contract stating what must be demonstrated before release, and organizes verification in a specification-first phase without access to the implementation and an implementation-aware phase based on mutation analysis, property-based testing, and fuzzing, with an assurance report that leaves the release decision to a human. We evaluate the framework in a pre-registered study on three stateful services, two of them written by third-party models, and an EvalPlus pilot. The builder's programs were correct, but its own tests missed subtle interactions: a verifier in a fresh context detected more of the 46 seeded faults than the builder's tests (Holm-corrected p = 0.006) and surfaced the ambiguities of the specification, at the price of rare false oracles. A verifier from another provider did not add detection.

title: OR-License: Evaluating LLM Agents as Real-World Operations Research Practitioners
abstract: Can large language model (LLM) agents deliver expert-level operations research (OR) solutions directly from original client materials, without prior expert reformulation? Existing OR benchmarks typically begin with self-contained descriptions or predefined optimization tasks, underrepresenting the translation of original business materials into professionally validated solutions. We introduce OR-License, an end-to-end benchmark of 31 instances across 10 industrial scenarios from paid OR engagements totaling USD 3.68 million. It preserves original requirements, input data, deliverable formats, and information boundaries after de-identification. To study information acquisition, we introduce ORSim, a controlled client simulator that discloses business facts without supplying OR expertise. Hidden evaluation checks feasibility and compares objective quality against original expert solutions accepted by clients before benchmark construction. Deployment-Adjusted Quality (DAQ) averages expert-relative quality across instances, assigning zero to infeasible deliveries. Across 11 frontier LLMs using coding-agent harnesses, several exceed the expert reference in conditional objective quality, but none matches its DAQ; the strongest primary Claude Code configuration achieves 88.39% strict feasibility and a DAQ of 0.87 against the expert reference of 1. Client information acquisition extends beyond clarification into solution development and validation, with some later stages showing higher confirmed issue-resolution proportions. Trajectory analysis identifies formulation and implementation failures, while task-equalized research-chain completion rates range from 24% to 45% across models on evaluable tasks. These findings motivate sustained information-gap resolution, faithful problem formulation, and evidence-linked self-improvement for reliable long-horizon agents.

title: Unbounded Losses, Unchecked Inputs: Measuring the Safeguards of LLM Options-Trading Agents
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents now place options orders at retail brokers, and developers publish open-source options agents faster than anyone has examined them. Prior security work on trading agents scored academic equities designs by whether an attacker can flip a buy-or-sell decision. We present the first measurement of the options agents that brokers and developers ship, scored by the safeguards they enforce and by the worst loss their documented order paths can reach. We screened 765 GitHub repositories, broker documentation, and the research literature and found 215 eligible repositories and 8 broker-native agent interfaces. We then scored 26 systems, including every broker interface and every open-source project with at least 20 stars, on seven robustness and eleven security safeguards with cell-level evidence. The ecosystem is new: 198 of the 215 repositories were created in 2026, and 129 (60.0%) appeared in the two weeks around one options-trading hackathon. Of the 22 systems that can place orders, 10 enforce a pre-trade limit outside the model, yet none of the 26 authenticate their text sources or cross-check market data. Of the 26, 17 can execute with no mandatory human step and 13 can reach unbounded loss, including 6 of the 8 broker interfaces. Because an attacker who writes the agent's inputs can move an order's strike, expiry, volatility, and legs while its direction stays correct, options agents need loss limits enforced at the order boundary.

title: When LLM-Generated Refactorings Ripple: An Empirical Study of Repository Adoption Readiness
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used to refactor source files, but file-local evaluations do not reveal changes to contracts, dependencies, or caller assumptions affecting repository adoption. To address this gap, we conduct 1,500 generation attempts across 150 production files from 15 open-source Java repositories, five LLM configurations, and two dependency-aware generation conditions: single-prompt refactoring and LangGraph-based multi-agent refactoring. Of these attempts, 1,455 yield complete candidates eligible for analysis. We evaluate these candidates using local changes, repository-facing structural indicators, detected caller impact, the behavioural-equivalence indicator, and available test evidence, and categorize them as Low-risk, Review-needed, High Contract/Dependency Risk, or Inconclusive. The results show that 1,365 candidates (93.8%) are classified as High Contract/Dependency Risk, whereas 106 (7.3%) have at least one detected broken downstream caller and 290 (19.9%) have a false behavioural-equivalence indicator; only eight satisfy the Low-risk criteria. Within the reason-covered subset, the High-risk rate decreases under more conservative dependency-delta thresholds, while 60 of the 65 candidates with conclusive targeted-test outcomes pass, including 50 classified as High risk. Paired analyses of 705 complete pairs identify no statistically significant generation-condition difference in the principal risk indicators, although model configurations differ in specific detected risk channels. These findings suggest that practitioners should treat LLM-generated refactorings as candidates requiring staged repository-level verification, while future research should validate screening and extraction precision and strengthen compilation, behavioural, and coordinated multi-file verification.

title: Pair-Aware Optimization: Coordinating Exploration and Refinement for Jailbreaking LLM Agents
abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents are vulnerable to adversarial inputs that induce attacker-specified malicious behaviors, commonly referred to as jailbreaking. Existing optimization-based jailbreak attacks primarily employ first-order (FO) methods that leverage gradient information or zeroth-order (ZO) methods that rely on function-value feedback. However, their complementarity and optimization ordering remain underexplored. We systematically investigate four strategies: pure ZO, pure FO, ZO->FO, and FO->ZO, and develop a ZO-FO framework that explores adversarial prefixes through ZO optimization and refines their corresponding suffixes through FO optimization. To coordinate the two processes, we introduce Pair-aware optimization, which retains multiple prefix candidates, conditionally refines their suffixes and selects among the resulting prefix-suffix pairs. We further investigate agent jailbreaking from a more general stochastic-generation perspective, where the same adversarial input can induce diverse reasoning trajectories and actions that a single greedy output cannot capture. Accordingly, we adopt consistent stochastic decoding during both optimization and evaluation. Experiments across malicious-instruction and malicious-environment benchmarks demonstrate that hybrid optimization improves attack effectiveness over single-optimizer methods, while optimization order substantially influences performance.

title: Teaching Code Agents to Ask Without Leaking Private Code
abstract: Local coding agents can extend their reach by consulting a stronger cloud model. Such consultations, however, often expose the repository's private identifiers, file paths, and source code. Host-side masking hides recognized identifiers but leaves the surrounding code and the agent's phrasing unchanged, while training for less disclosure risks suppressing consultation or producing questions too vague to answer. We propose utility-verified abstraction (UVA), which teaches the agent to describe private entities by their role and type while retaining the technical details an expert needs. From solved repair trajectories, we rewrite each question into this form and keep the rewrite only if it discloses fewer private entities and the repair, replayed from the same execution state with the repair trajectories. Across two benchmarks, the trained agent consults more often than before training. On repository-level issue repair, it solves 37.6% of issues, against 25.3% for the same model working alone, a gain from the training as a whole rather than from consultation alone. Its questions disclose 3.7-fold fewer private entities and 1.4-fold less verbatim code than the untrained agent's questions to the same expert.

title: The One-Pixel of Reasoning: One Truthful Relation Is Enough to Mislead LLM Agents
abstract: Can one sentence manipulate an agent's belief by targeting a single implicit warrant linking evidence to a conclusion? In this paper, we introduce the one-relation attack (ORA), a novel cognitive attack on this inferential relation. ORA localizes a critical implicit warrant and performs a one-relation intervention using a single source-grounded sentence that qualifies this warrant and steers the agent toward an incorrect belief. Across eighteen models on biomedical inference and vulnerability detection, best-of-$10 attacks overturn initially correct answers at mean rates of 54.9% for proprietary and 80.0% for open-weight models. Attacks also transfer without victim feedback, and paired controls support the roles of targeting and qualification. Moreover, successful sentences can pass source-support checks and evade identification, and multi-agent debate raises team error from 50.0% to 59.5% in our balanced stress test. These findings establish implicit warrants as a cognitive attack surface for manipulating agents' beliefs.

title: Peer Pressure: Execution-Verified Co-Evolution of Attacker and Defender Populations for Code Security
abstract: LLM code agents increasingly ship code with little oversight, yet defenders trained on static vulnerability datasets fall behind adapting adversaries. We co-train attacker and defender instead, and let execution decide every reward: an attacker (Red) edits a real repository and earns nothing unless its patch applies, builds, passes the tests, completes its development task and reproduces a real exploit in an isolated container, whose path also labels the entry point, the critical operation and the trace between them. Peer-Relative Policy Optimization (PRPO) makes both sides populations of LoRA adapters over one frozen base and credits each against same-role peers that faced an identical condition, placing the population inside the policy-gradient baseline rather than the opponent pool, with a tournament preserving diversity. Matching cancels the condition's difficulty: at equal coverage it is worth 2.3 points of balanced accuracy over a baseline computed on other conditions, and it matches a within-policy control at half the verifier spend.
